title: Resolution of time concepts in temporal databases
research_question: Which temporal dimensions and validity concepts are necessary to preserve database history precisely and losslessly when information may be entered retroactively, proactively, corrected, or recorded after a delay?
methodology: The paper takes a formal temporal-database approach, defining temporal validity and extending it to interpretation-based validity in order to distinguish previously conflated notions of time. It analyzes what temporal dimensions are required to preserve multiple past states under different kinds of update. The authors then characterize object history along valid time and sketch how such history can be implemented in the relational data model.

key_findings.finding: Three distinct temporal concepts are required for the paper's account of precise and lossless preservation of temporal database information.
Valid time and transaction time alone cannot correctly represent retroactive and proactive updates; event time is additionally required.

The combination of event time, valid time, and transaction time is presented as adequate for preserving past states generated by retroactive updates, proactive updates, error corrections, and delayed updates.
Temporal validity and interpretation-based validity are introduced to clarify the semantics of different time concepts and to define an object's evolution along the valid-time dimension.
The paper sketches a relational-data-model implementation for retaining object history rather than treating the formal distinctions only as abstract semantics.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible from the primary publication source during this review, so the formal definitions, proofs, examples, and implementation details could not be independently inspected.
The accessible evidence establishes a formal adequacy argument rather than an empirical performance evaluation.
The implementation is described in the abstract as a sketch, so no claim about production-scale feasibility or performance can be established from the accessible text.
No released software, experimental dataset, or quantitative evaluation metric is identified in the accessible abstract.
raw_claims: The paper distinguishes three temporal concepts for lossless temporal information preservation.
Temporal validity is formally distinguished from an extended interpretation-based notion of validity.
Preserving multiple historical database states motivates the need to separate different temporal dimensions.
Valid time and transaction time are insufficient by themselves for retroactive and proactive updates.
Event time provides information needed to model those update cases correctly.
Event, valid, and transaction times together are presented as sufficient for preserving histories involving retroactive and proactive updates.
The same three-dimensional treatment covers histories affected by error correction and delayed recording.
Object history can be characterized along valid time using the proposed validity semantics.
The paper includes a sketch of how retained history can be represented in a relational data model.
